posts.title: Why your case never sees a platform
posts.excerpt: From hotel bedroom door to evening room, your heavy suitcase travels by dedicated road van so you can board scenic trains with free hands and complete peace of mind.
posts.content:
If you ask anyone over sixty what causes the greatest anxiety on a rail holiday, the answer is rarely the train ride itself. It is the moments in between: hauling a heavy suitcase across a crowded station concourse, finding an elevator that actually works, negotiating the narrow gap between a moving train and the edge of the platform, and lifting luggage onto an overhead rack while passengers press from behind. At Kisha Rail Holidays, we resolved that problem before we ever ran our first tour. On our lines, your suitcase never sees a station platform.

The system is simple, quiet, and carried out every morning while you enjoy breakfast. Each guest is asked to pack their main suitcase and leave it outside their hotel bedroom door by 08:45. At that moment, your responsibility for your luggage ends for the day. Ravi Menon, who oversees our luggage and road logistics, arrives outside each room with his trolley. He loads every suitcase into our dedicated white transfer van, checks the luggage roster against his master list, and drives directly to our evening hotel.

While Ravi takes the road network, our sixteen guests take the train. Because your main suitcase is already en route, you walk out of the hotel lobby carrying only a small day bag containing your book, woollen scarf, reading glasses, and any medication you might require before dinner. When our private transfer coach pulls up at the station, you walk directly to the platform unencumbered. Your hands are free to hold a handrail, steady yourself with a walking stick, or simply hold your partner's hand.

Boarding the train becomes an unhurried pleasure rather than an obstacle. When our train pulls in, your tour manager—such as Amara Okafor on the Lakes & Viaduct Line—unfolds a sturdy metal step at the carriage door and stands ready with a steady forearm. Without the burden of twenty kilograms of luggage, stepping aboard requires only a single confident step. Inside the carriage, our group seats are already reserved together, with window seats shared in turn throughout the holiday. You sit down, hang your coat on the peg, and watch the scenery unfold through the glass.

Meanwhile, Ravi is already arriving at our next hotel. He unloads each case, liaises with the hotel reception staff, and oversees the luggage delivery directly into each guest room using the hotel lift. By 16:30, when our train arrives at our destination and we transfer to the hotel, your suitcase is already waiting safely inside your room. You collect your room key, take the lift to your floor, and find your belongings resting on the luggage bench, ready for unpacking.

Helen Marsh instituted this rule when she founded the company in 2009. Having ridden every railway line herself, she knew that true relaxation on a scenic holiday requires dignity and ease at every transfer. By separating passenger travel from luggage transport, we ensure that our guests experience only the romance and beauty of rail travel, completely free from the physical strain of heavy bags.

posts.title: Crossing the Arlen viaduct at walking pace
posts.excerpt: The Lakes & Viaduct Line takes the long stone viaduct slowly, and the group has the window seats in turn.
posts.content:
On Day 2 of the Lakes & Viaduct Line the train slows for the Arlen viaduct and the whole carriage goes quiet. Amara Okafor keeps the window seats in turn, so that everyone has the view of the valley once before lunch.

Nothing is rushed: at most three hours on a train in any day, and the rest of the afternoon is a level walk or a free hour in the square.

posts.title: A night in the sleeper, from the cabin door
posts.excerpt: Tomasz Nowak on the one night of the Northern Pines Sleeper spent in a cabin with two lower berths.
posts.content:
On the Northern Pines Sleeper one night of the eight is spent in a sleeper cabin. Tomasz Nowak checks every cabin before the guests board, and lower berths are kept for anyone who asks.

The morning begins with coffee at the cabin door and a day sheet read aloud once, as on every tour.
